paragraphs.heading: Chemistry in three dimensions
paragraphs.text: Stereochemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies how the atoms of a molecule are arranged in space, and how that arrangement can be manipulated. Its central subject is stereoisomers: molecules that share a molecular formula and the same order of bonded atoms, called the constitution, but whose atoms sit in different places in space. That is why it is also called 3D chemistry, since the prefix stereo- means three-dimensionality. It applies to every kind of compound and ion, organic and inorganic alike.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of isomer
paragraphs.text: These isomers fall into two types. Enantiomers are mirror images that cannot be laid exactly on top of each other. Diastereomers, also called diastereoisomers, are all the other types. The field reaches into biological, physical and supramolecular chemistry, and it also studies how these molecules react, a part known as dynamic stereochemistry.

paragraphs.heading: Drawing molecules on paper
paragraphs.text: Rather than a detailed 3D picture, chemists use a few simple standard ways to show where atoms sit around a stereocenter. In one, a solid wedge marks a bond pointing toward the viewer, a dashed or hashed bond marks one pointing away, and a plain line marks one lying in the plane of the molecule. A Fischer projection draws the four bonds of a tetrahedral atom straight across or straight up and down: vertical bonds point away from the viewer and horizontal ones point toward. To name arrangements without ambiguity, the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priority rules rank the atoms around a stereochemical region in a standard order. Devised in 1966, they give a chiral center an R or S label.

paragraphs.heading: The thalidomide lesson
paragraphs.text: Stereochemistry matters a great deal in medicine, especially for drugs, and thalidomide is the example most often given. First made in Germany in 1957, it was prescribed to pregnant women for morning sickness, and it turned out to badly damage embryos as they grew, causing deformed limbs in babies. Several proposed explanations involve its (R) and (S) enantiomers having different biological roles. Yet the body converts one form into the other, a process called racemization, so giving just one form still yields both, and calling one version safe is wrong. The disaster did much to push for strict testing of medicines before they reach the public.

paragraphs.heading: A gentler example
paragraphs.text: Ibuprofen also exists as (R) and (S) isomers. Only the (S) form actually eases inflammation and pain. Thalidomide itself is still used today, notably against cancer and leprosy. Strict rules and controls now keep it away from pregnant women to prevent deformities.

paragraphs.heading: Where the field began
paragraphs.text: Organic stereochemistry began in 1815, when Jean-Baptiste Biot saw that organic molecules in a solution or a gas could rotate the plane of polarized light. Even so, Louis Pasteur is usually called the first stereochemist. In 1842 he found that tartaric acid salts from wine-making vessels rotated polarized light, while salts from other sources did not, and this was the only physical property that set the two apart. In 1874 van 't Hoff and Le Bel explained such rotation by a tetrahedral arrangement of the atoms bound to carbon. Lord Kelvin introduced the word chiral in 1904.
